title: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (January 2027) — the first edition published after the 2026-12-11 funding cliff, and the one that actually carries the publication risk
source: EST: eia.gov/outlooks/steo/release_schedule.php, fetched direct 2026-09-08 (HTTP 200, 54,906 bytes) by the eia-steo-2026-12-08 never-assessed initial research, whose table row reads "January 2027 | 01/12/2027" with a blank Notes cell. Reproduces independently from the same page's stated rule ("the first Tuesday following the first Thursday of each month", with a Federal holiday on the preceding Monday pushing the release to Wednesday): 2027-01-07 is a Thursday, the following Tuesday is 01-12, and 01-11 is not a Federal holiday, so no adjustment applies. Release window is stated on the same page as 12:00-12:15 pm ET. Filed estimate on the two counts every EIA entry on this calendar records, neither of them date doubt: this calendar defines no `confirmed` prefix for the EIA (the standing schema gap eia-steo-2026-09-09 named), and a discovering lane never self-confirms an event it found in-sweep
notes: Discovered during eia-steo-2026-12-08's never-assessed initial research (2026-09-08), off the same EIA release-schedule primary that dates the December edition. Proposed because that session moved a risk rather than killing it, and this is where the risk actually lands. The October sibling proposed 12-08 as 'the last edition before the funding cliff' and wrote the appropriations exposure into its notes; on the primary that exposure does not reach 12-08 at all — PL 119-103 section 106 funds agencies through 2026-12-11, so the December edition publishes three days INSIDE the funded window. THIS edition is the first STEO on the far side of the cliff, and cr-expiry-2026-12-11 explicitly declines to inherit government-funding-deadline-2026-09-30's aversion base case, calling the December branch genuinely open on the 2018-19 lame-duck analogue (35 days, begun 2018-12-21). So a lapse beginning 00:00 2026-12-12 would be ~32 days old by 01-12. The mitigating precedent travels with the risk rather than instead of it, and it is strong: EIA published the October 2025 STEO on 2025-10-07, seven days into the October 2025 lapse. Two further reasons this edition is worth a slot beyond calendar completeness. It follows the 2026-12-09 FOMC SEP decision and the 2026-12-10 CPI print by a month, so it is the first energy forecast written with the December rate path known. And it is the January edition — the point in the annual cycle where the STEO's forecast horizon rolls forward a year, which if it holds makes 01-12 the first publication of a 2028 forecast line; that horizon-roll claim is NOT verified from a primary by the proposing session and is flagged for the owning lane to check rather than asserted. Filed `low` on the sibling entries' reasoning: a forecast publication sets no policy and moves no equity tape.
